rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reads “straight path” in annexation, meaning the religion that is upright.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر الصادق: صراط مستقيم بالإضافة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Ḥasan’s and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s reading, “the path of those” is a definite apposition to an indefinite, like “a straight path, God’s path.”
rows.anchor: فعلى قراءة الحسن والضحاك يكون صراط الذين بدل معرفة من نكرة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Ṣādiq’s and the majority’s readings, “the path of those” is an apposition of one definite to another, clarifying the previously somewhat vague “straight path.”
rows.anchor: وعلى قراءة الصادق وقراءات الجمهور تكون بدل معرفة من معرفة صراط الذين بدل شيء من شيء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This apposition restates the request for guidance, making it firmer and more emphatic by directing it to the path of those God favored.
rows.anchor: وجيء بها للبيان لأنه لما ذكر قبل اهدنا الصراط المستقيم كان فيه بعض إبهام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rare interpretation says the second path is not the first, as though a conjunction had been read; interpreters differ over its identification.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب القول أن الصراط الثاني ليس الأول، بل هو غيره،

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad identifies the favored path as knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
rows.anchor: قيل هو العلم بالله والفهم عنه، قاله جعفر بن محمد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the path as fulfilling religious obligations and following the Prophetic sunna.
rows.anchor: وقيل التزام الفرائض واتباع السنن، وقيل هو موافقة الباطن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the path harmony between inward and outward states in the fullness of divine favor.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو موافقة الباطن للظاهر في إسباغ النعمة.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read “the path of those whom You favored” without the relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ: صراط من أنعمت عليهم، ابن مسعود، وعمر، وابن الزبير، وزيد بن علي.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to identify those favored as believers.
rows.anchor: أو المؤمنون، قاله ابن عباس. أو الأنبياء والمؤمنون،

rows.speaker: وكيع
rows.claim: Wakīʿ identifies those favored as prophets and believers, or as Muslims.
rows.anchor: أو الأنبياء والمؤمنون، أو المسلمون، قاله وكيع، أقوال،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the majority’s identification to the four groups named in 4:69, and also records Ibn ʿAbbās’s view that they are believers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: والجمهور أراد صراط النبيين والصديقين والشهداء والصالحين،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies the favored people as the Companions of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم.

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group identifies them as the believing Israelites.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: مؤمنو بني إسرائيل.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses’s followers before they altered the message.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أصحاب موسى قبل أن يبدلوا.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda restricts those favored to the prophets.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الأنبياء خاصة. وقال أبو العالية:

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya identifies those favored as Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبو بكر وعمر، انتهى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording leaves divine favor unrestricted, so it encompasses every kind of favor; the text supplies no basis for narrowing it to a particular favor.
rows.anchor: ولم يقيد الأنعام ليعم جميع الأنعام، أعني عموم البدل.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say God favored them by creating them for felicity; others say He rescued them from ruin, or guided them to follow the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنعم عليهم بخلقهم للسعادة، وقيل بأن نجاهم من الهلكة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi writers add many restrictions, but the wording does not support assigning the favor one particular restriction.
rows.anchor: وروي عن المتصوفة تقييدات كثيرة غير هذه، وليس في اللفظ ما يدل على تعيين قيد.

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites affirm that God bestows favor on unbelievers, while others deny it.
rows.anchor: واختلف هل لله نعمة على الكافر؟ فأثبتها المعتزلة ونفاها غيرهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Upon them” is syntactically accusative, as are prepositional phrases attached to an active verb or equivalent.
rows.anchor: وموضع عليهم نصب، وكذا كل حرف جر تعلق بفعل، أو ما جرى مجراه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active “You favored” gently appeals to God’s prior generosity to secure acceptance of the plea for continued guidance, like reminding a benefactor of his customary kindness.
rows.anchor: وبناء أنعمت للفاعل استعطاف لقبول التوسل بالدعاء في الهداية وتحصيلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual Arabic construction changes the verb’s person with an attached pronoun, though another dialect keeps it unchanged.
rows.anchor: وانقلاب الفاعل مع المضمر هي اللغة الشهرى، ويجوز إقرارها معه على لغة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer asks that guidance continue: praising God, worshipping Him, and seeking His help already indicate guidance, but the worshipper asks for its permanence.
rows.anchor: ومضمون هذه الجملة طلب استمرار الهداية إلى طريق من أنعم الله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ghayr” is masculine singular by default; feminine agreement may follow its form or its meaning, and it denotes some kind of difference.
rows.anchor: غير مفرد مذكر دائما وإذا أريد به المؤنث جاز تذكير الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ghayr” is originally an adjective, can mark exception, must be annexed, and cannot take the definite article or become definite merely through annexation.
rows.anchor: ومدلوله المخالفة بوجه ما، وأصله الوصف، ويستثنى به ويلزم الإضافة

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj holds that “ghayr” becomes definite by annexation when the thing it differs from is a single definite referent.
rows.anchor: ومذهب ابن السراج أنه إذا كان المغاير واحدا تعرف بإضافته إليه

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh allows a normally non-defining annexation to become defining when it is intended as such, making “ghayr” definite with a definite complement.
rows.anchor: وتقدم عن سيبويه أن كل ما إضافته غير محضة، قد يقصد بها التعريف،

rows.speaker: البيانيون
rows.claim: Rhetoricians say “ghayr” or “mithl” is nearly required before the predicate in examples where it means anyone sharing the stated quality.
rows.anchor: وزعم البيانيون أن غير أو مثلا في باب الإسناد إليهما مما يكاد يلزم تقديمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetoricians mean that anyone sharing the described quality is expected by analogy and custom to act in the stated way.
rows.anchor: ولكنهم يعنون أن كل من كان مثله في الصفة كان من مقتضى القياس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Al-maghdūb ʿalayhim” means those incurred anger; anger can also mean turning away because that is one of its consequences.
rows.anchor: المغضوب عليهم، الغضب: تغير الطبع لمكروه، وقد يطلق على الإعراض لأنه من ثمرته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle lā serves negation, command, or redundancy; contrary to the Kufans, it is not a noun.
rows.anchor: لا حرف يكون للنفي وللطلب وزائدا، ولا يكون اسما خلافا للكوفيين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love.
rows.anchor: والضلال سلوك سبيل غير القصد، ضل عن الطريق سلك غير جادتها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The non-majority genitive reading of “ghayr”; al-Khalīl reports Ibn Kathīr’s accusative reading, also attributed to ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, and Ibn al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: وروى الخليل عن ابن كثير النصب، وهي قراءة عمر، وابن مسعود، وعلي،

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī analyzes the genitive as an apposition to “those” or to the pronoun in “upon them,” but Abū Ḥayyān says both are weak because “ghayr” is adjectival.
rows.anchor: فالجر على البدل من الذين، عن أبي علي، أو من الضمير في عليهم، وكلاهما ضعيف،

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh permits the genitive as an adjective, taking “ghayr” as definite through annexation; Abū Ḥayyān also reports Ibn al-Sarrāj’s narrower rationale and rejects a generic-plural rationale.
rows.anchor: أو على النعت عن سيبويه، ويكون إذ ذاك غير تعرفت بما أضيفت إليه،

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī and others take the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from “those”; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it because the annexed complement has no syntactic position.
rows.anchor: أو من الذين قاله المهدوي وغيره، وهو خطأ، لأن الحال من المضاف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic line means its speaker is unlike people easily deceived; reversing the placement of “ghayr” reverses the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: غيري بأكثر هذا الناس ينخدع غرضه أنه ليس ممن ينخدع ويغتر،

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj, and others treat the accusative as a disconnected exception; al-Qurrāʾ object because of the following lā.
rows.anchor: على الاستثناء، قاله الأخفش، والزجاج وغيرهما، وهو استثناء منقطع،

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: Al-Qurrāʾ allow lā to be extra only after a prior negation, citing poetic usage and 17:61; Abū Ḥayyān discusses competing analyses of the cited poems.
rows.anchor: قال لأن لا، لا تزاد إلا إذا تقدم النفي، نحو قول الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against interpreters who call lā redundant in the verse about “my generosity,” he argues it is the object of “refused”; “al-bukhl” is an apposition or purpose object.
rows.anchor: بل الأظهر أن لا مفعول بأبى، وأن لفظة لا لا تتعلق بها،

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: A further analysis attributed to al-Khalīl supplies an implied “I mean” before “ghayr.”
rows.anchor: وقيل انتصب غير بإضمار أعني وعزى إلى الخليل، وهذا تقدير سهل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Upon them” is nominative as the passive subject of “incurred anger”; grammarians discuss when a prepositional phrase may stand as passive subject.
rows.anchor: وعليهم في موضع رفع بالمغضوب على أنه مفعول لم يسم فاعله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lā before “those astray” reinforces negation; placing it in the coordination prevents “those astray” from being mistaken as part of “those You favored.”
rows.anchor: ولا في قوله: ولا الضالين لتأكيد معنى النفي، لأن غير فيه النفي،

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar and Ubayy read “and not those astray” with “ghayr”; variants are also reported for the case ending of rāʾ, distinguishing the two groups.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر وأبي وغير الضالين، وروي عنهما في الراء في الحرفين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī introduces a grammatical example to illustrate the semantic closeness of ghayr and lā.
rows.anchor: أتى الزمخشري بمسألة ليبين بها تقاربهما فقال: وتقول أنا زيدا غير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that “ghayr” allows an object before it, just as lā does, and uses this to establish their grammatical and semantic similarity.
rows.anchor: لكنهم تسمحوا في العامل المضاف إليه غير، فأجازوا تقديم معموله على غير إجراء لغير مجرى لا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls al-Zamakhsharī’s argument very weak: the construction is disputed, similarity in meaning does not transfer syntax, and “أنا زيدا غير ضارب” is unattested.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذهب إليه الزمخشري مذهب ضعيف جدا، بناه على جواز أنا زيدا لا ضارب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplying an omitted “path” before “ghayr” yields weak analyses, including an adjective before its apposition or repeated apposition.
rows.anchor: وقدّر بعضهم في غير المغضوب محذوفا، قال التقدير غير صراط المغضوب عليهم،

rows.speaker: أيوب السختياني
rows.claim: Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads “wa-laḍ-ḍāllīn” with a hamza in place of the long vowel to avoid two adjacent vowelless letters.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أيوب السختياني: ولا الضألين، بإبدال الألف همزة فرارا من التقاء الساكنين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza substitution occurs in words such as dāba and shāba, but it is too rare to be treated as a productive rule, despite Abū al-Fatḥ’s dialect argument.
rows.anchor: ومع ذلك فلا ينقاس هذا الإبدال لأنه لم يكثر كثرة توجب القياس،

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd records dāba and shāba as dialect examples; he first thought ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd had misread until he heard the forms from Arabs.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد: سمعت عمرو بن عبيد يقرأ فيومئذ لا يسأل عن ذنبه إنس ولا جان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting favor in the verbal relative clause of “those” fixes it to an established act, while the participial “incurred anger” leaves its time broad; the past verb specifies confirmed favor.
rows.anchor: وجعل الإنعام في صلة الذين، والغضب في صلة أل، لأن صلة الذين تكون فعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive “incurred anger” avoids directly attributing anger to God in a humble plea for kindness, and prepares the parallel ending “those astray.”
rows.anchor: وبناه للمفعول، لأن من طلب منه الهداية ونسب الإنعام إليه لا يناسب نسبة الغضب إليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended favor is religious; “those angered” and “those astray” are general categories of everyone who incurs anger and goes astray.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالإنعام، الإنعام الديني، والمغضوب عليهم والضالين عام في كل من غضب عليه وضل.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians.
rows.anchor: وقيل المغضوب عليهم اليهود، والضالون النصارى، قاله ابن مسعود، وابن عباس، ومجاهد،

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: This Jews-and-Christians interpretation is also reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be followed if authentic.
rows.anchor: وروي هذا عن عدي بن حاتم، عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other identifications say the angered are Jews and polytheists; Sufi restrictions also circulate but are not supported by the verse’s wording.
rows.anchor: وقيل اليهود والمشركون، وقيل غير ذلك. وقد روي في كتب التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine anger can mean the will to punish, an attribute of essence given God’s prior knowledge, or the act of inflicting punishment, an attribute of action.
rows.anchor: والغضب من الله تعالى إرادة الانتقام من العاصي لأنه عالم بالعبد قبل خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anger precedes misguidance despite resulting from it because it is paired antithetically with favor; the order also suits the verse-ending cadence and the conjunction itself implies no sequence.
rows.anchor: وقدم الغضب على الضلال، وإن كان الغضب من نتيجة الضلال ضل عن الحق فغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the groups mean Jews and Christians, Jews come first because they appeared earlier or are more hostile.
rows.anchor: فالتقديم إما للزمان أو لشدة العداوة، لأن اليهود أقدم وأشد عداوة من النصارى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poetry illustrates the hamza substitution; if it is a dialect as Abū al-Fatḥ says, Abū Ḥayyān reasons that the substitution should be productive.
rows.anchor: إذا ما العوالي بالعبيط احمأرت وقول الآخر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening is especially elegant whether the basmala is counted as the first verse or “Praise be to God” is; both begin the discourse fittingly.
rows.anchor: فإن كان أولها بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم، على قول من عدها منها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamd intensifies praise by making it comprehensive.
rows.anchor: النوع الثاني: المبالغة في الثناء، وذلك لعموم أل في الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some rhetoricians call “Praise be to God” a statement whose intended force is command, like “no doubt in it” meaning “do not doubt.”
rows.anchor: النوع الثالث: تلوين الخطاب على قول بعضهم، فإنه ذكر أن الحمد لله صيغته صيغة الخبر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “to God” restricts all praise to Him, and the annexation “Master of the Day of Judgment” underscores His sole dominion when other dominions vanish.
rows.anchor: النوع الرابع: الاختصاص باللام التي في لله، إذ دلت على أن جميع المحامد مختصة به،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative reading of “al-ḥamd” involves ellipsis; grammarians differ over whether its omitted governing word repeats the noun or is another word.
rows.anchor: النوع الخامس: الحذف، وهو على قراءة من نصب الحمد ظاهر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some analyses posit omitted “path” before “not angered,” while other syntactic choices create many further ellipses in the sūra.
rows.anchor: ومنه حذف صراط من قوله غير المغضوب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra uses fronting and delay in “we worship, we seek help” and in “those angered, those astray.”
rows.anchor: التقديم والتأخير، وهو في قوله نعبد، ونستعين، والمغضوب عليهم، والضالين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apposition “the path of those whom You favored” is explicit clarification after the initially vague “straight path.”
rows.anchor: النوع السابع: التفسير، ويسمى التصريح بعد الإبهام، وذلك في بدل صراط الذين من الصراط المستقيم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to direct address in “You alone we worship,” “You alone we seek help,” and “guide us” is iltifāt.
rows.anchor: النوع الثامن: الالتفات، وهو في إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين، اهدنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Guide us” asks for the continuance of guidance, not its initial acquisition alone.
rows.anchor: النوع التاسع: طلب الشيء، وليس المراد حصوله بل دوامه، وذلك في اهدنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra strings together attributes to specify, praise, or blame the described referents, and ends with parallel cadence in the paired phrases.
rows.anchor: النوع الحادي عشر: التسجيع، وفي هذه السورة من التسجيع المتوازي،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan disliked calling the sūra “Mother of the Book”; Ibn Sīrīn disliked “Mother of the Qurʾān,” while the majority allow the latter.
rows.anchor: وكره الحسن أن يقال لها أم الكتاب، وكره ابن سيرين أن يقال لها أم القرآن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is consensus that al-Fātiḥa has seven verses, apart from an unconsidered dissent.
rows.anchor: والإجماع على أنها سبع آيات إلا ما شذ فيه من لا يعتبر خلافه.

rows.speaker: الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون
rows.claim: The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices.
rows.anchor: عد الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية، ولم يعدوا أنعمت عليهم،

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: In an anomalous count, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd treats “You alone we worship” as a verse, giving eight verses.
rows.anchor: وشذ عمرو بن عبيد، فجعل آية إياك نعبد، فهي على عده ثمان آيات،

rows.speaker: حسين الجعفي
rows.claim: Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī anomalously claims the sūra has six verses.
rows.anchor: وشذ حسين الجعفي، فزعم أنها ست آيات.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says 17:87, “We gave you seven of the oft-repeated,” settles the verse count.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقول الله تعالى: ولقد آتيناك سبعا من المثاني هو الفصل في ذلك.

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: All deny that the basmala at each sūra’s opening is a verse, except Ibn al-Mubārak, who says it is a verse in every sūra.
rows.anchor: ولم يختلفوا في أن البسملة في أول كل سورة ليست آية، وشذ ابن المبارك فقال: إنها آية في كل سورة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports of the sūra’s letter count and alleged occasions of revelation do not constitute a sound occasion of revelation; reported basmala virtues are of uncertain reliability.
rows.anchor: وذكر المفسرون عدد حروف الفاتحة، وذكروا سبب نزولها ما لا يعد سبب نزول.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fātiḥa has many reported names; most ancillary discussions, including “Āmīn,” are outside tafsīr unless they identify an ambiguity, authentic revelation occasion, or abrogation.
rows.anchor: وذكروا أن الفاتحة تسمى الحمد، وفاتحة الكتاب، وأم الكتاب، والسبع المثاني،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the one who purifies succeeds and that the Hereafter is better was not abrogated: it held in earlier revelations and in the final dispensation.
rows.anchor: لفي الصحف الأولى، لم ينسخ إفلاح من تزكى، والآخرة خير وأبقى في شرع

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read “ṣuḥuf” with a ḍamma on ḥāʾ; al-Aʿmash, Hārūn, and ʿIṣma report a sukūn, identified as Tamīmī usage.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: الصحف بضم الحاء كالحرف الثاني والأعمش وهرون وعصمة، كلاهما عن أبي عمرو:

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the name Ibrāhīm; several transmitters report variants, including Abū Rajāʾ without the alif and yāʾ and Abū Mūsā and Ibn al-Zubayr’s “Ibrāhām.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: إبراهيم بألف وبياء والهاء مكسورة وأبو رجاء: بحذفهما والهاء مفتوحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of the scrolls of Abraham and Moses was already given in Sūrat al-Najm.
rows.anchor: وتقدم في والنجم الكلام على صحف إبراهيم وموسى عليهما الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa, whom the author thinks is the botanist, calls ḍarīʿ shibriq, a poor pasture that gives grazing animals neither fat nor flesh.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حنيفة وأظنه صاحب النبات، الضريع: الشبرق، وهو مرعى سوء لا تعقد السائمة عليه شحما ولا لحما،

rows.speaker: ابن عزارة الهذلي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAzāra al-Hudhalī’s verse uses ḍarīʿ for a thorny plant in a hollow, where a camel is described as gaunt and weak-legged.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول ابن عزارة الهذلي: وحبسن في هزم الضريع فكلها

rows.speaker: أبو ذؤيب
rows.claim: Abū Dhuʾayb’s verse says the grazing animals eat fresh shibriq until it dries into ḍarīʿ, after which the lean camels leave it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو ذؤيب: رعى الشبرق الريان حتى إذا ذوى ... وصار ضريعا بان عنه النحائص

rows.speaker: بعض اللغويين
rows.claim: Some lexicographers define ḍarīʿ as dried ʿurfuj once crushed.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض اللغويين: يبيس العرفج إذا تحطم.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj calls ḍarīʿ a plant like ʿawsaj.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: هو نبت كالعوسج.

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl describes it as a green, foul-smelling plant cast up by the sea.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: نبت أخضر منتن الريح يرمي به البحر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Namāriq are cushions; the singular is namraqa, pronounced with either ḍamma or kasra on nūn and rāʾ.
rows.anchor: النمارق: الوسائد، واحدها نمرقة بضم النون والراء وبكسرهما.

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s verse couples honored elders and youths with faces on aligned couches and cushions.
rows.anchor: وقال زهير: كهولا وشبانا حسانا وجوههم ... على سرر مصفوفة ونمارق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zarābī are broad, luxurious rugs; al-Farrāʾ calls them plush carpets and gives two pronunciations for the singular zarība.
rows.anchor: الزرابي: بسط عراض فاخرة. وقال الفراء: هي الطنافس المخملة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The earth was spread” means it was flattened and made walkable.
rows.anchor: سطحت الأرض: بسطت ووطئت.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is Meccan and follows the preceding sūra’s command to remind and mention of fire and the Hereafter with a question about the overwhelming event.
rows.anchor: هي مكية. ولما ذكر فيما قبلها فذكر

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān and the majority understand al-ghāshiya as the calamity that overwhelms people with the terrors of the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: والغاشية: الداهية التي تغشى الناس بشدائدها يوم القيامة، قاله سفيان والجمهور.

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb identify al-ghāshiya as Hell, which covers its inhabitants and faces.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير ومحمد بن كعب: النار، قال تعالى: وتغشى وجوههم النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question arrests the listener’s attention so that he receives the report; another interpretation takes it as a reminder of the Prophet’s divinely taught knowledge, and another reads “has it come?”
rows.anchor: وهذا الاستفهام توقيف، وفائدته تحريك نفس السامع إلى تلقي الخبر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Faces that day” means the day on which the overwhelming event covers them; the tanwīn stands for the relative clause implicit in al-ghāshiya.
rows.anchor: وجوه يومئذ: أي يوم إذ غشيت، والتنوين عوض من الجملة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāshiʿa means humbled and abased.
rows.anchor: خاشعة: ذليلة. عاملة ناصبة،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatāda say the faces toil in Hell because they arrogantly refused work in the world.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والحسن وابن جبير وقتادة: عاملة في النار، ناصبة تعبة فيها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The toil in Hell includes dragging chains, wading through fire like camels in mud, and ceaselessly climbing and descending its slopes.
rows.anchor: قيل. وعملها في النار جر السلاسل والأغلال، وخوضها في النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Jubayr also say the people labored in worldly misguidance; the verse applies to Christian clergy, idolaters, and every strenuous unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا وزيد بن أسلم وابن جبير: عاملة في الدنيا ناصبة فيها

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Suddī read “working, weary” in the accusative as blame, while the majority read both nominative.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة والسدي: عاملة ناصبة بالنصب على الذم، والجمهور برفعهما.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read taṣlā with fatḥa on tāʾ; Abū Rajāʾ, Ibn Muḥayṣin, and the two readers read it with ḍamma, while Khārija doubles lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ: تصلى بفتح التاء وأبو رجاء وابن محيصن والأبوان: بضمها وخارجة:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ḥāmiyya means fiercely heated; Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid say āniya means that its heat has reached its limit.
rows.anchor: حامية: مسعرة آنية قد انتهى حرها، كقوله: وبين حميم آن

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd instead reads āniya as present and ready, from the verb meaning that something has arrived.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: حاضرة لهم من قولهم: آنى الشيء حضر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls ḍarīʿ a tree of fire.
rows.anchor: والضريع، قال ابن عباس: شجر من نار.

rows.speaker: الحسين
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn and others identify ḍarīʿ with zaqqūm.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين: وجماعة الزقوم.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, and Mujāhid identify the Hell plant as shibriq; other views are ʿabsharaq, fresh ʿurfuj, or a valley in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا وقتادة وعكرمة ومجاهد: شبرق النار. وقيل: العبشرق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ḍarīʿ is ghislin or zaqqūm, the exclusive food statements need not conflict: each food can belong to a different group; alternatively the plants differ.
rows.anchor: والضريع، إن كان الغسلين والزقوم، فظاهر ولا يتنافى الحصر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows “does not fatten or relieve hunger” to modify either “food” or “ḍarīʿ”; the food is thorn, unlike nourishing human fare.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: لا يسمن مرفوع المحل أو مجروره على وصف طعام أو ضريع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects attaching the clause to the negated “food,” since that construction implies other food that does nourish; it can modify an implied “being of ḍarīʿ.”
rows.anchor: وأما رفعه على وصفه لطعام فلا يصح، لأن الطعام منفي ولا يسمن، منفي فلا يصح تركيبه،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī proposes that no food exists at all because ḍarīʿ is not food even for beasts, making the exception disconnected; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the connected reading because all food is something consumed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أو أريد أن لا طعام لهم أصلا، لأن الضريع ليس بطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite subject “faces” is licensed by the detailed contrast with the earlier faces that were humbled.
rows.anchor: وجوه يومئذ ناعمة: صح الابتداء في هذا وفي قوله: وجوه يومئذ خاشعة بالنكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāʿima means either beautiful and fresh or enjoying comfort.
rows.anchor: ناعمة لحسنها ونضارتها أو متنعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed are content with their worldly obedience because it earns them Paradise.
rows.anchor: لسعيها راضية: أي لعملها في الدنيا بالطاعة، راضية إذا كان ذلك العمل جزاؤه الجنة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A high garden is elevated both in location and in rank.
rows.anchor: في جنة عالية: أي مكانا ومكانة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several readers take “no idle speech is heard” passively with “idle” nominative, construed as a word, group of speakers, or verbal noun; another group reads the verb with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: لا تسمع مبنيا للمفعول، لاغية: رفع، أي كلمة لاغية، أو جماعة لاغية،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Abū Jaʿfar, Qatāda, Ibn Sīrīn, and other readers use active second-person “you do not hear,” with “idle” accusative; its subject may be general or the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والحسن وأبو رجاء وأبو جعفر وقتادة وابن سيرين ونافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flowing spring may be a generic kind meaning springs, or a specially named spring honored by mention.
rows.anchor: فيها عين جارية: عين اسم جنس، أي عيون، أو مخصوصة ذكرت تشريفا لها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raised couches may be elevated in rank or physically high so their occupants see their blessings, or “raised” may mean hidden away.
rows.anchor: فيها سرر مرفوعة: من رفعة المنزلة أو رفعة المكان ليرى ما خوله ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cups are set out with drinks ready, placed within reach, or positioned at the edges of the springs.
rows.anchor: وأكواب موضوعة: أي بأشربتها معدة لا تحتاج إلى مالىء، أو موضوعة بين أيديهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cushions are lined up next to one another for leaning and reclining.
rows.anchor: ونمارق مصفوفة: أي وسائد صف بعضها إلى جنب بعض للاستناد إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The carpets are spread here and there throughout the gathering places.
rows.anchor: وزرابي مبثوثة: متفرقة هنا وهنا في المجالس.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After dividing people into blessed and wretched at Judgment, God cites familiar created signs as evidence for the wise Maker.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى أمر القيامة وانقسام أهلها إلى أشقياء وسعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camels gather many benefits: meat, milk, transport across vast distances, grazing on many plants, enduring thirst, obedience, rising under heavy loads, and responsiveness to beautiful sound.
rows.anchor: فإنه اجتمع فيها ما تفرق من المنافع في غيرها، من أكل لحمها، وشرب لبنها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel is the Arabs’ most valuable possession, used for blood money and lavish gifts; poets praise those who give a hundred.
rows.anchor: ولكونها أفضل ما عند الغرب، جعلوها دية القتل، ووهبوا المائة منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning camels alongside sky, mountains, and earth fits what Arabs constantly saw in their valleys and demonstrates that the Creator’s work spans all kinds of beings.
rows.anchor: وناسب التنبيه بالنظر إليها وإلى ما حوت من عجائب الصفات، ما ذكر معها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic maxim states that every thing bears a sign pointing to the One Creator.
rows.anchor: وفي كل شيء له آية ... تدل على أنه واحد

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says “camels” here can mean clouds, since they come in strings, are driven along, and sometimes resemble camels or ostriches; he adduces a poem.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العباس: المبرد: الإبل هنا السحاب، لأن العرب قد تسميها بذلك،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that the cloud interpretation need not make camel a dictionary name for cloud; it may be a figurative comparison common in poetry.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ولم يدع من زعم أن الإبل السحاب إلى قوله إلا طلب المناسبة،

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read al-ibil with kasra on bāʾ and a light lām; al-Aṣmaʿī reports a sukūn and ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās a doubled lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: الإبل بكسر الباء وتخفيف اللام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan defends mention of camels: they eat date stones and fodder and yield milk, whereas Arabs scarcely knew elephants, which cannot be eaten, ridden, or milked.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: خص الإبل بالذكر لأنها تأكل النوى والقت وتخرج اللبن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibil is feminine and has no singular of the same form; its diminutive is abīla, its plural ābāl, and unusual derivatives include taʾabbala and mā ābalu.
rows.anchor: والإبل لا واحد له من لفظه وهو مؤنث، ولذلك إذا صغر دخلته التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How it was created” is an interrogative clause apposed to “camels”; the verb is suspended from its ordinary object by the question about manner.
rows.anchor: وكيف خلقت: جملة استفهامية في موضع البدل من الإبل، وينظرون: تعدى إلى الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab usage permits a preposition before “how”; since the question is about manner, the verb is “created,” while suspension makes it unlike a genuine question.
rows.anchor: على أن العرب قد أدخلت إلى على كيف، فحكى أنهم قالوا: انظر إلى كيف يصنع.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read the verbs as passives; ʿAlī, Abū Ḥaywa, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read first-person active forms with the objects omitted, “I created, raised, set up, spread them.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: خلقت: رفعت، نصبت سطحت بتاء التأنيث مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky is raised far without pillars, mountains set firmly without shifting, and earth spread flat as a bed for those who move over it.
rows.anchor: رفعت رفعا بعيد المدى بلا عمد، نصبت نصبا ثابتا لا تميل ولا تزول

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Hārūn double the ṭāʾ in saṭaḥat; the majority pronounce it light.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: سطحت خفيفة الطاء والحسن وهارون: بشدها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remind means the Prophet should not be troubled by their refusal to look; his task is reminder, as in the declaration that his duty is only conveyance.
rows.anchor: ولما حضهم على النظر، أمر رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم بتذكيرهم فقال: فذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are not a controller over them” means not a coercive ruler, comparable to “you are not a tyrant over them.”
rows.anchor: لست عليهم بمصيطر: أي بمسلط، كقوله: وما أنت عليهم بجبار

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ṣād; variants use sīn, an emphatic z-like sound, or fatḥa on ṭāʾ, the last attributed to Tamīmī usage.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بالصاد وكسر الطاء، وابن عامر في رواية، ونطيق عن قنبل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb sayṭara is transitive, as shown by its passive form; few Arabic agent nouns share its pattern.
rows.anchor: وسيطر متعد عندهم ويدل عليه فعل المطاوعة وهو تسطر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “Except those who turn away and disbelieve” may be a connected exception from the Prophet’s lack of control, or from the command to remind with an intervening parenthesis.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: إلا حرف استثناء فقيل متصل، أي فأنت مسيطر عليه.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes the exception disconnected and the passage a truce later abrogated by the sword verse.
rows.anchor: وقيل: منقطع، وهي آية موادعة نسخت بآية السيف.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Qatāda, and Zayd ibn Aslam read “alā” as an attention-getting particle instead of the exception “illā.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وزيد بن علي وقتادة وزيد بن أسلم: ألا حرف تنبيه واستفتاح،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greater punishment is the punishment of Hell.
rows.anchor: والعذاب الأكبر هو عذاب جهنم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read iyābahum with a light yāʾ; Abū Jaʿfar and Shayba double it and offer several morphological analyses.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: إيابهم بتخفيف الياء مصدر آب وأبو جعفر وشيبة: بشدها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī derives the doubled reading from “awāb,” by analogy with words whose medial wāw changes to yāʾ and assimilates.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح، وتبعه الزمخشري: يكون أصله إوابا مصدر أوب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the “awāb” account because an assimilated wāw preceded by kasra is protected from the proposed substitution; the pattern examples remain unassimilated.
rows.anchor: فأما كونه مصدر أوب فإنه لا يجوز، لأنهم نصوا على أن الواو الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects comparing the doubled form to dīwān: Arabic did not attest an assimilated *dawān, and dīwān itself is anomalous rather than a productive model.
rows.anchor: وأما تشبيه الزمخشري بديوان فليس بجيد لأنهم لم ينطقوا بها في الوضع مدغمة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests deriving the form from a doubled hamza in aʾwaba, softened and then assimilated; Abū Ḥayyān says the regular outcome is iyāb.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: ويصح أن يكون من أأوب، فيجيء إيوابا، سهلت الهمزة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With assimilation, the softened hamza yields a yāʾ beside the root wāw; the wāw then changes to yāʾ and assimilates, producing iyāb.
rows.anchor: بل اللازم إذا اعتبر الإدغام أن يكون إيابا، لأنه قد اجتمعت ياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes the fronted “to Us” and “upon Us” as restriction: return and reckoning belong exclusively to God.
rows.anchor: ولما كان من مذهب الزمخشري أن تقديم المعمول يفيد الحصر، قال معناه: أن إيابهم ليس إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān reports that al-Zamakhsharī’s exclusivity follows from his theory that fronting the complement gives restriction; only God is obliged, in the sense of wisdom, to reckon.
rows.anchor: ولما كان من مذهب الزمخشري أن تقديم المعمول يفيد الحصر

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that in the last ten nights the Prophet tightened his waist-wrapper, kept vigil, and woke his family.
rows.anchor: قالت عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا دخل العشر

rows.speaker: التبريزي
rows.claim: Al-Tabrīzī says scholars agree that the ten nights are Ramadan’s final ten, whose importance suits the solemn oath.
rows.anchor: قال التبريزي: اتفقوا على أنه العشر الأواخر، يعني من رمضان، لم يخالف فيه أحد،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī identifies the ten nights with the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijja and explains their indefinite form as highlighting a special subset or excellence.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وأراد بالليالي العشر عشر ذي الحجة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says al-Zamakhsharī’s questions about indefiniteness and lack of the definite article are understandable but his answers are incoherent verbiage.
rows.anchor: أما السؤالان فظاهران، وأما الجواب عنهما فلفظ ملفق لا يعقل منه معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thirty-six explanations of “the even and the odd” have been recorded elsewhere, but Abū Ḥayyān declines to reproduce so many.
rows.anchor: والشفع والوتر: ذكر في كتاب التحرير والتحبير فيها ستة وثلاثين قولا

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين
rows.claim: A report from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn traces to the Prophet the interpretation that the even and odd refer to the prayers, some even and some odd.
rows.anchor: وعن عمران بن حصين، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «هي الصلوات، منها الشفع ومنها الوتر»

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب
rows.claim: A report from Abū Ayyūb traces to the Prophet the interpretation that the even is the Day of ʿArafa and the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Sacrifice night.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو أيوب عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم: «الشفع يوم عرفة ويوم الأضحى، والوتر: ليلة النحر»

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: A report from Jābir traces to the Prophet the reversed interpretation: the even is the Day of Sacrifice and the odd is the Day of ʿArafa.
rows.anchor: وروى جابر عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم: «الشفع يوم النحر، والوتر يوم عرفة»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Jābir report interprets dawn as morning and the ten nights as the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijja, also Ibn ʿAbbās’s and ʿIkrima’s view, preferred by al-Naḥḥās.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الحديث تفسيره عليه الصلاة والسلام الفجر بالصبح والليالي العشر بعشر النحر

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās says the Jābir report through Abū al-Zubayr is authentic and better-attested than the report from ʿImrān; ʿArafa is odd as the ninth day and Sacrifice even as the tenth.
rows.anchor: وقال حديث أبي الزبير عن جابر: هو الذي صح عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī notes that interpreters offered many low-value explanations, nearly exhausting every possible pair of even and odd things.
rows.anchor: والزمخشري ثلاثة أقوال، ثم قال: وقد أكثروا في الشفع والوتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “for food” can mean “for feeding,” though Abū Ḥayyān prefers supplying an omitted “giving of,” yielding “giving food.”
rows.anchor: على طعام، يجوز أن يكون بمعنى إطعام، كالعطاء بمعنى الإعطاء، والأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic heirs withheld inheritance from women and young children, claiming only those who fought and protected the clan deserved shares.
rows.anchor: وتأكلون التراث، كانوا لا يورثون النساء ولا صغار الأولاد، فيأكلون نصيبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ in turāth replaces a wāw, as in takla and tukhma from their corresponding verbs.
rows.anchor: والتراث تاؤه بدل من واو، كالتكلة والتخمة من توكلت ووخمت.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says heirs knowingly consumed the deceased’s ill-gotten wealth, mixing lawful and unlawful money and squandering it because they had not earned it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانوا يأكلون ما جمعه الميت من الظلمة وهم عالمون بذلك يجمعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rebukes their conduct; the passage then warns them and evokes their regret over neglecting worldly deeds.
rows.anchor: كلا: ردع لهم عن ذلك وإنكار لفعلهم. ثم أتى بالوعيد وذكر تحسرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkan dakkan is an accusative of manner meaning pulverizing repeatedly, like the idiom “door by door.”
rows.anchor: دكا دكا: حال كقولهم: بابا بابا، أي مكررا عليهم الدك.

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Judge Mundhir ibn Saʿīd says “your Lord came” means His becoming manifest to creation then, not movement from place to place; the same applies to the calamity and blast.
rows.anchor: وجاء ربك، قال القاضي منذر بن سعيد: معناه ظهوره للخلق هنالك، وليس بمجيء نقلة،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes “came” as God’s power and authority.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وجاء قدرته وسلطانه.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats the coming as a metaphor for the appearance of signs of God’s power, like a king whose personal arrival displays more awe than his army.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هو تمثيل لظهور آيات اقتداره وتبيين آثار قدرته وسلطانه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic term “angels” includes the angels of every heaven, who are reported to form ranks around the earth at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: والملك اسم جنس يشمل الملائكة. وروي أنه ملائكة كل سماء تكون صفا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī pictures the angels descending heaven by heaven, rank upon rank, surrounding jinn and humankind.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: صفا صفا تنزل ملائكة كل سماء فيصطفون صفا بعد صف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Hell is brought” parallels the statement that Hell is exposed for all to see.
rows.anchor: وجيء يومئذ بجهنم، كقوله تعالى: وبرزت الجحيم لمن يرى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes “that day” an apposition to “when,” with “remember” governing both; Abū Ḥayyān notes the apparent attribution to Sībawayh but prefers an implicitly repeated governor.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وعامل النصب فيهما يتذكر،

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say the regretful person gains no benefit from remembrance then; if he had heeded in earthly life it would have helped him in the next life.
rows.anchor: أي منفعة الذكرى، لأنه وقت لا ينفع فيه التذكر، لو اتعظ في الدنيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and others take “my life” to mean earthly life; another group says it means the grave life they had denied.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري وغيره: أو وقت حياتي في الدنيا، كما تقول: جئت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that regret proves people had the choice to obey and were not compelled; Abū Ḥayyān identifies this as Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وهذا أبين دليل على أن الاختيار كان في أيديهم

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: The claim that a divine oath’s wāw never appears with an explicit verb is not consensus: Ibn Kaysān permits “I swear, by God, Zayd stands.”
rows.anchor: فليس هذا الحكم مجمعا عليه، بل قد أجاز ابن كيسان التصريح بفعل القسم مع الواو،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The theory that coordinating wāws act as substitutes for the omitted oath governor rests on treating a conjunction as a governing particle, which Abū Ḥayyān does not prefer.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: والواوات العواطف نوائب عن هذه إلخ، فمبني على أن حرف العطف عامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The real grammatical difficulty is identifying what governs future-time idhā after an oath, as in several neighboring sūras.
rows.anchor: والذي نقوله: إن المعضل هو تقرير العامل في إذا بعد الإقسام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted oath verb cannot govern future idhā because an utterance of swearing is performative in the present and its time conflicts with a future dependent.
rows.anchor: فإذا ظرف مستقبل، لا جائز أن يكون العامل فيه فعل القسم المحذوف، لأنه فعل إنشائي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An implied noun such as “rising of the star” cannot solve the problem, since the noun denotes a present action and likewise mismatches a future-time dependent.
rows.anchor: ولا جائز أن يكون ثم مضاف محذوف أقيم المقسم به مقامه، أي: وطلوع النجم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath object itself cannot govern idhā, and an implied circumstantial “being” fails because temporal adverbs cannot modify concrete entities as states or predicates.
rows.anchor: ولا جائز أن يعمل فيه نفس المقسم به لأنه ليس من قبيل ما يعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs is generic, as shown by the following “inspired it” and by the contrast between whoever purifies and whoever corrupts it; its rectification completes its rational faculty.
rows.anchor: ونفس وما سواها: اسم جنس، ويدل على ذلك ما بعده من قوله: فألهمها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī suggests the indefinite “a soul” might mean Adam alone; Abū Ḥayyān says this is far-fetched because the subsequent descriptions require a generic soul.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: لم نكرت النفس؟ قلت: فيه وجهان: أحدها: أن يريد نفسا خاصة

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr glosses “inspired it” as “imposed it.”
rows.anchor: فألهمها، قال ابن جبير:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God made the soul know; Ibn Zayd says He explained to it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: عرفها. وقال ابن زيد: بين لها.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says God enabled the soul for piety; another explanation is that He taught it and gave it power to acquire either sin or piety.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: وفقها للتقوى، وألهمها فجورها: أي خذلها، وقيل: عرفها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets inspiration of sin and piety as understanding good and evil and being enabled to choose either, supported by the agency in the next verses.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ومعنى إلهام الفجور والتقوى: إفهامها وإعقالها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls al-Zamakhsharī’s interpretation a covert Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: انتهى، وفيه دسيسة الاعتزال.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and others take “successful is whoever purifies it” as the oath’s answer, with an omitted emphatic lām after the long intervening text.
rows.anchor: قد أفلح من زكاها، قال الزجاج وغيره: هذا جواب القسم، وحذفت اللام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī instead supplies “God will destroy them”—the Meccans for denying Muḥammad as Thamūd denied Ṣāliḥ—and treats purification as a digression, not the oath’s answer.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: تقديره ليدمدمن الله عليهم، أي على أهل مكة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification is the soul’s growth and emergence through good works; corruption hides and diminishes it through sins.
rows.anchor: وزكاؤها: ظهورها ونماؤها بالعمل الصالح، ودساها: أخفاها وحقرها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and others take the subject of “purifies” and “corrupts” to be the relative “whoever.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن فاعل زكى ودسى ضمير يعود على من

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second analysis makes God the subject of purifying and corrupting, with feminine agreement referring to the implied soul; a Prophetic supplication after reciting the verse supports this reading.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون ضمير الله تعالى، وعاد الضمير مؤنثا باعتبار المعنى من مراعاة التأنيث.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī attacks the attribution of the verbs to God as a Qadarite slander; Abū Ḥayyān replies that the interpreter was Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: هذا، وقائل ذلك هو بحر العلم عبد الله بن عباس،

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq and others take “the latter is better” to mean the two abodes, this world and the next.
rows.anchor: وللآخرة خير لك من الأولى: يريد الدارين، قاله ابن إسحاق وغيره.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows that the verse may contrast the Prophet’s circumstances before and after the sūra, promising victory and success.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يريد حالتيه قبل نزول السورة وبعدها، وعده تعالى بالنصر والظفر،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī links the verse to the preceding denial of abandonment: God continues to reveal to and honor His beloved, then promises greater honors in the Hereafter, including precedence, testimony, elevated ranks, and intercession.
rows.anchor: لما كان في ضمن نفي التوديع والقلى أن الله مواصلك بالوحي إليك

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority place the promised gift in the Hereafter; Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet is satisfied when none of his household enter Hell, and elsewhere describes a thousand palaces with their provisions and servants.
rows.anchor: ولسوف يعطيك ربك فترضى، قال الجمهور: ذلك في الآخرة. وقال ابن عباس: رضاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view placing the gift in this world, such as the conquest of Mecca, can be included; the promise best encompasses both worldly victories and stored reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في الدنيا بفتح مكة وغيره، والأولى أن هذا موعد شامل لما أعطاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “for the Hereafter” and “you will be given” strengthens the assertions; the second has an omitted subject, “you will surely be given.”
rows.anchor: واللام في وللآخرة لام ابتداء أكدت مضمون الجملة، وكذا في ولسوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Did He not find you” means “know you”; the Prophet’s father died when he was six months in the womb, and his mother when he was eight, after which Abū Ṭālib raised him.
rows.anchor: ألم يجدك: يعلمك، يتيما: توفي أبوه عليه الصلاة والسلام وهو جنين،

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet was orphaned by both parents so he would owe no creature anything.
rows.anchor: وقيل لجعفر الصادق: لم يتم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من أبويه؟

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports that yatīm can mean uniquely peerless, as a rare pearl, and interprets the verse as saying Muḥammad had no equal among Quraysh; Abū Ḥayyān dismisses the interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ومن يدع التفاسير أنه من قولهم درة يتيمة،

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read fa-āwā as a quadriliteral verb; Abū al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī reads the triliteral fa-awā, meaning that God showed mercy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فآوى رباعيا وأبو الأشهب العقيلي: فأوى ثلاثيا، بمعنى رحم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He found you astray” cannot mean error opposed to guidance, since prophets are protected from that.
rows.anchor: ووجدك ضالا: لا يمكن حمله على الضلال الذي يقابله الهدى، لأن الأنبياء معصومون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Muḥammad became lost in Mecca’s passes as a child, then God returned him to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هو ضلاله وهو في صغره في شعاب مكة، ثم رده الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other accounts say he was lost from his wet nurse Ḥalīma or on the Syrian journey with Abū Ṭālib; Abū Ḥayyān rejects interpretations improper to attribute to prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضلاله من حليمة مرضعته. وقيل: ضل في طريق الشام حين خرج به أبو طالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān recalls a dream interpretation: God found the Prophet’s people astray and guided them through him; this requires an omitted possessive, like “ask the town.”
rows.anchor: ووجدك، أي وجد رهطك، ضالا، فهداه بك.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ʿāʾilan as poor; al-Yamānī reads the emphatic ʿayilan, and poetry distinguishes the verbs meaning becoming poor and having many dependents.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: عائلا: أي فقيرا. قال جرير:

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Mujāhid? [sic] Muqātil says God enriched the Prophet through contentment with the provision He gave.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: فأغنى رضاك بما أعطاك من الرزق.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other interpretations say God enriched him through contentment and patience, or through sufficiency.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أغناك بالقناعة والصبر. وقيل: بالكفاف.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says not to subdue or despise the orphan.
rows.anchor: فلا تقهر، قال مجاهد: لا تحتقره. وقال ابن سلام: لا تستزله.

rows.speaker: ابن سلام
rows.claim: Ibn Sallām says not to humiliate the orphan; Sufyān says not to wrong him by mishandling his property; al-Farrāʾ says not to withhold his due.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان: لا تظلمه بتضييع ماله. وقال الفراء: لا تمنعه حقه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of al-sāʾil is a beggar; do not rebuke him, but give to him or dismiss him kindly.
rows.anchor: وأما السائل: ظاهره المستعطي، فلا تنهر: أي تزجره، لكن أعطه أو رده ردا جميلا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says not to speak harshly to the asker; this instruction corresponds to the blessing of being enriched.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: لا تغلظ عليه،

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abū al-Dardāʾ, al-Ḥasan, and others take the asker as one asking about knowledge and religion, linking the instruction to God’s guidance.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الدرداء والحسن وغيرهما: السائل هنا: السائل عن العلم والدين،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Kalbī interpret speaking of the Lord’s blessing as reciting the Qurʾān and conveying the message.
rows.anchor: وأما بنعمة ربك فحدث، قال مجاهد والكلبي: معناه بث القرآن

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq identifies the blessing to proclaim as prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق: هي النبوة.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says announcing blessings is both thanking God and publicizing the favors of shelter, guidance, provision, and more.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: التحديث بالنعم: شكرها وإشاعتها، يريد ما ذكره من نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three commands answer three blessings: care for the orphan, kindness to the asker, then—at the sūra’s climax—proclaim the greatest blessing, guidance; their order follows the Prophet’s life after orphanhood and his protected adulthood.
rows.anchor: ويظهر أنه لما تقدم ذكر الامتنان عليه بذكر الثلاثة، أمره بثلاثة:

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad defines safʿ as a forceful tug; a poetic use describes someone seizing a horse’s forelock.
rows.anchor: السفع، قال المبرد: الجذب بشدة، وسفع بناصية فرسه:

rows.speaker: عمرو بن معد يكرب
rows.claim: A verse by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib uses sāfiʿ for one seizing a horse while the people shout.
rows.anchor: قال عمرو بن معد يكرب: قوم إذا كثر الصياح رأيتهم ... من بين ملجم مهره أو سافع

rows.speaker: مؤرج
rows.claim: Muʾarrij says nādī means a gathering according to Quraysh usage; the related nadā also means a council or assembly.
rows.anchor: وقال مؤرج: معناه الأخذ بلغة قريش، النادي والندى: المجلس،

rows.speaker: أعرابية
rows.claim: A Bedouin woman’s phrase “master of his gathering” illustrates nādī as a meeting place.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الأعرابية: سيد ناديه وثمال عافيه،

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s verse uses andiya for assemblies visited by talk and action.
rows.anchor: وقال زهير: وفيهم مقامات حسان وجوههم ... وأندية ينتابها القول والفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zabāniya are the angels of punishment; some say the plural has no singular of the same form.
rows.anchor: الزبانية: ملائكة العذاب، فقيل: جمع لا واحد له من لفظه،

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda gives the singular as zabniya, modeled like ḥadriya or ʿafriya; al-Kisāʾī instead gives zabnī, reanalyzed as a nisba.
rows.anchor: واحدهم زبنية على وزن حدرية وعفرية، قاله أبو عبيدة.

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Akhfash give zābin as the singular; the word also describes someone forceful, supported by poetry and ʿUtba ibn Abī Sufyān’s saying about war.
rows.anchor: قال عيسى بن عمر والأخفش: واحدهم زابن، والعرب تطلق هذا الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Meccan sūra begins with the first Qurʾanic revelation, sent in Ḥirāʾ according to Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī; the report from Jābir that al-Muddaththir came first and Abū Maysara’s claim that al-Fātiḥa came first are unsound.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية، وصدرها أول ما نزل من القرآن، وذلك في غار حراء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, citing Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, also calls it the first sūra revealed; most commentators instead say al-Fātiḥa first, then al-Qalam.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري، عن ابن عباس ومجاهد: هي أول سورة نزلت، وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the previous sūra’s account of humanity created in the best form and its later decline, this passage recalls human development and divine favors before describing rebellion and its afterlife outcome.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر فيما قبلها خلق الإنسان في أحسن تقويم، ثم ذكر ما عرض له

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read iqraʾ with a hamza; al-Aʿshāʾ, transmitting from Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, drops it by analogy with the imperfect verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: اقرأ بهمزة ساكنة والأعشى، عن أبي بكر، عن عاصم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ may mark an instrument or accompaniment, with an omitted object meaning “read what is revealed”; alternatively God’s name is the object, or one reads the basmala at each sūra’s opening.
rows.anchor: والظاهر تعلق الباء باقرأ وتكون للاستعانة، ومفعول اقرأ محذوف،

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes bāʾ as “upon,” as in the command to board the ark in God’s name.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: الباء بمعنى على، أي اقرأ على اسم الله،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes “in the name of your Lord” a circumstantial accusative: begin by saying the basmala, then read; Abū Ḥayyān notes the analysis is also attributed to Qatāda.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: محل باسم ربك النصب على الحال، أي اقرأ مفتتحا باسم ربك،

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda regards the bāʾ as extra, meaning “mention your Lord”; he also regards “name” as extra, yielding “read with your Lord’s aid.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الباء صلة، والمعنى اذكر ربك. وقال أيضا: الاسم صلة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The choice of “your Lord” evokes the one who nurtured and cared for the Prophet; direct address indicates exclusive intimacy, with no lord for him but God.
rows.anchor: وجاء باسم ربك، ولم يأت بلفظ الجلالة لما في لفظ الرب من معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Creator excludes the idols that Arabs called lords; the unexpressed object is universal, meaning that He created everything.
rows.anchor: ثم جاء بصفة الخالق، وهو المنشئ للعالم لما كانت العرب تسمي الأصنام أربا.
